claims.text: Tungsten particles should be pre-coated with a uniform copper layer by vapor-phase deposition before consolidation.
Vapor-phase copper pre-coating will reduce interfacial voids in consolidated W–Cu composites.
Vapor-phase copper pre-coating will reduce phase separation in consolidated W–Cu composites.
Vapor-phase copper pre-coating will improve W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding will enhance thermal transport.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding will improve mechanical durability under irradiation.
The starting tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions have native surface oxides.
Conventionally SPS-processed W–Cu composites exhibit interfacial voids.
Conventionally sintered W–Cu composites exhibit phase separation or elemental inhomogeneity.
The copper coating acts as an interfacial bridge between tungsten and the copper matrix.
The copper coating cleans the tungsten surface.
The copper coating facilitates intimate diffusion bonding with the copper matrix.
Copper pre-coating improves the wettability of tungsten during sintering.
Copper pre-coating reduces native oxide barriers on tungsten surfaces.
Reduced void formation and phase separation improve load-transfer resilience under irradiation.
Relative to uncoated SPS W–Cu composites, coated samples will have a more homogeneous microstructure and lower void fraction.
Relative to uncoated SPS W–Cu composites, coated samples will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to uncoated SPS W–Cu composites, coated samples will retain greater mechanical durability during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Processing below copper's boiling point and under inert or reducing atmosphere will maintain copper integrity.
The long-term stability of the copper coating under extreme irradiation and extended thermal cycling is unvalidated.
